concepts.title: @RestController and Request Mapping
concepts.description: @RestController marks a class as a web endpoint whose methods write their return values directly to the HTTP response body instead of resolving a view, and the @xMapping family of annotations declares which URL paths, HTTP methods, and parameters each handler method actually responds to.
learningObjectives: Explain what @RestController does and how it differs from plain @Controller.
Explain how DispatcherServlet and its HandlerMapping route an incoming HTTP request to a specific handler method.
Use @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, and @DeleteMapping and explain their relationship to the generic @RequestMapping.
Extract path segments and query parameters using @PathVariable and @RequestParam, including required vs. optional handling.
Explain what HTTP status results when no handler matches a request's path or method.
Predict why two handler methods with overlapping mappings cause a startup-time failure rather than a runtime routing decision.

sections.heading: @Controller vs. @RestController
sections.body:
`@Controller` is Spring MVC's base stereotype for a class that handles web requests. Historically, a `@Controller` method returns a *logical view name*, a string like `"orders/list"`, which a `ViewResolver` then maps to a template (JSP, Thymeleaf, etc.) to render as HTML. That suits a server-rendered web application, but it is the wrong default for a JSON REST API, where you want a method's return value serialized directly into the response body, not interpreted as a template name.

`@RestController` is a meta-annotation that combines `@Controller` with `@ResponseBody`. `@ResponseBody`, applied to a method (or, via `@RestController`, implicitly to every method in the class), tells Spring MVC: 'do not treat this return value as a view name; write it to the HTTP response body, running it through the appropriate `HttpMessageConverter` first.' Before `@RestController` existed (it arrived in Spring 4.0), building a REST endpoint meant writing `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody` on every handler method. `@RestController` removes that repetition for classes where *every* method produces a body.

sections.heading: How Requests Get Routed: DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping
sections.body:
Spring MVC follows the *front controller* pattern: a single servlet, `DispatcherServlet` (registered automatically by Spring Boot's web autoconfiguration, tying back to the previous module), receives every HTTP request that reaches the application. At startup, Spring builds an index (a `HandlerMapping`) of every `@RequestMapping`-family-annotated method across every `@Controller`/`@RestController` bean in the context, recording each one's path pattern, HTTP method, and any additional conditions (headers, params, `consumes`, `produces`).

When a request arrives, `DispatcherServlet` consults this index to find the single best-matching handler method, based on the request's path and HTTP method (and those additional conditions, when specified), and dispatches to it. Because the index is built at startup, two handlers registered under the same mapping are caught there (covered further down).

sections.heading: @RequestMapping and Its HTTP-Method-Specific Shortcuts
sections.body:
`@RequestMapping` is the general-purpose mapping annotation; you can write `@RequestMapping(path = "/orders", method = RequestMethod.GET)` and it works. In practice, almost nobody writes it that way for a single HTTP method, because Spring provides pre-specialized shortcuts (`@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@DeleteMapping`, `@PatchMapping`), which are themselves meta-annotated with `@RequestMapping` and a fixed `method` value. They exist for readability; `@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")` says what it does at a glance, in a way `@RequestMapping(value = "/orders/{id}", method = RequestMethod.GET)` does not.

A common pattern is to put a base path on the *class* with `@RequestMapping("/api/orders")`, and then let each method's mapping supply only the sub-path relative to that base: `@GetMapping("/{id}")` on a method inside that class resolves to the full path `/api/orders/{id}`. This keeps a whole resource's routes visually grouped and avoids repeating the shared prefix on every method.

sections.heading: Extracting Data From the Request: @PathVariable and @RequestParam
sections.body:
`@PathVariable` binds a segment of the URI template to a method parameter: given a mapping of `@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")`, a parameter `@PathVariable Long id` receives whatever value appeared in that position of the actual request path, converted to a `Long`. `@RequestParam` binds a query-string parameter (or a form field on certain request types): `@GetMapping("/orders")` with `@RequestParam(required = false) String status` reads `?status=SHIPPED` off the URL, and, because `required` is explicitly set to `false`, leaves the parameter `null` rather than rejecting the request if `status` is omitted entirely (the default for `required` is `true`, which causes a `400 Bad Request` if the parameter is missing and no `defaultValue` is supplied).

By default, Spring matches a `@PathVariable`/`@RequestParam` parameter to the URI template variable or query parameter with the *same name* as the Java parameter itself, which relies on the compiled bytecode retaining parameter names (enabled by the `-parameters` compiler flag, which Spring Boot's default Maven/Gradle build plugins turn on for you). Name the binding yourself (`@PathVariable("id") Long orderId`) if you can't be sure that flag is set (IDE builds and hand-rolled compiler settings are the usual culprits), or where the Java parameter name and the URL segment name are meant to differ.

sections.heading: What Happens When Nothing Matches
sections.body:
If no registered handler's path pattern matches the incoming request path at all, the client receives `404 Not Found`. If a path pattern *does* match, but no handler registered for that path accepts the request's HTTP method, the client receives `405 Method Not Allowed` instead, which tells the caller the path exists but doesn't support that verb.

A subtler case is two handler methods whose mappings collide. If two methods declare the *same* mapping, for example both `@GetMapping("/products/{id}")`, the second registration fails while the index is being built, and the application stops at startup with `IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping`.

Startup checking has a limit, though. It compares the mappings as declared, so `/products/{id}` and `/products/{productId}` count as different and both get registered. A request to `/products/42` then matches both equally well, and Spring throws `IllegalStateException: Ambiguous handler methods mapped for '/products/42'` at request time, which the client sees as a 500. A test that requests each route catches this; starting the application does not.

examples.title: A Minimal REST Controller
examples.explanation: OrderController receives its OrderService dependency through the constructor, as covered in the Core Concepts module: controllers are beans too, and are wired the same way as any other. The class-level @RequestMapping("/api/orders") establishes a shared base path; getOrder's @GetMapping("/{id}") resolves to the full route GET /api/orders/{id}, with the {id} segment bound to the id parameter via @PathVariable. listOrders's bare @GetMapping resolves to GET /api/orders itself, and its status parameter is bound from an optional query string parameter (required = false), so a request to GET /api/orders with no query string at all still matches this method, just with status equal to null. It's OrderService's own job, not Spring's, to decide what a null status filter means.

examples.title: An Ambiguous Mapping Failure at Startup
examples.explanation: Both methods declare the same mapping, GET /products/{id}, so Spring detects the conflict while building its handler index and refuses to start. The different Java method names don't help, because they aren't part of the mapping, and neither are the names chosen for path variables: those are used only afterward, to bind a value to a parameter once a single handler has been selected. Failing at startup is the better outcome, because otherwise one method would shadow the other and the bug would only show up the first time someone requested /products/42. Renaming the second placeholder to {productId} would be worse than leaving it: the two patterns would then be registered as different mappings, the application would start, and the first GET /products/42 would fail with a 500 because both handlers match it equally well.

examples.title: Explicit Binding When Names Don't Match
examples.explanation: getOrder's URI template variable is named id, but the Java method parameter is named orderId. Without @PathVariable("id"), Spring would look for a URI variable called orderId and fail the request with MissingPathVariableException (a 500). Passing the name makes the binding correct whatever the Java parameter is called. search's @RequestParam similarly renames the bound query parameter to q (so the actual URL is /orders/search?q=...) while giving it a defaultValue of an empty string, meaning a request with no q parameter at all still succeeds, with query bound to "" rather than null, so the method needs no null check. The literal path /orders/search also wins over /orders/{id} for that URL, because Spring prefers the more specific pattern.

misconceptions.description: @RestController writes a method's return value to the response exactly as-is, similar to a raw servlet writing text directly -- there's no real conversion step happening.
misconceptions.clarification: Every return value from a @RestController method passes through Spring MVC's HttpMessageConverter chain before it becomes bytes on the wire. For a domain object, that typically means MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter serializing it to JSON; for a bare String, a different converter (StringHttpMessageConverter) writes it as literal text. Which converter gets used depends on the request's Accept header and the mapping's declared produces value, matched against which converters are registered (Jackson's exists because the web starter put Jackson on the classpath).
misconceptions.fact: Every return value from a @RestController method passes through Spring MVC's HttpMessageConverter chain before it becomes bytes on the wire.

misconceptions.description: Two handler methods with different parameter types or different parameter names can share the exact same path and HTTP method without conflicting, because Spring can tell them apart by their Java signatures.
misconceptions.clarification: Request mapping matches purely on path pattern shape, HTTP method, and any explicitly declared conditions (headers, params, consumes, produces). It has no visibility into a handler method's parameter types or parameter names at all when deciding whether two mappings conflict. Two GET methods on the same path pattern are ambiguous to Spring however different their Java signatures look, and the application fails at startup with an Ambiguous mapping error. If only the variable names differ ({id} vs {productId}), startup succeeds but the first matching request fails as ambiguous.

exercises.prompt: This application fails to start with an 'Ambiguous mapping' error involving ProductController. Find and fix the conflict so both endpoints can coexist and behave distinctly.
hints: Spring identifies a mapping by its path pattern and HTTP method -- Java method names play no role, and renaming a {placeholder} would only move the failure from startup to the first request.
Both methods currently describe exactly the same thing: GET on /products/<one path segment>. What could make them describe genuinely different routes instead?
Give the second endpoint a distinguishing, literal path segment (like /products/{id}/details) rather than another single variable segment at the same position.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original two mappings both describe GET requests against /products/<single segment>, and the mapping is identical in path pattern and HTTP method, so registering the second one fails at startup. Adding a distinguishing literal segment, /products/{id}/details, changes the pattern (two segments instead of one after /products/), so the two mappings are no longer ambiguous: GET /products/42 routes to getProduct, and GET /products/42/details routes to getProductDetails.

exercises.prompt: Given this handler method, what does calling GET /search (no query string) return, and what does calling GET /search?category=shoes return?
hints: required = false means the request is NOT rejected when the category query parameter is absent -- but what value does the parameter get bound to in that case?
For an object type like String (as opposed to a primitive like int), an absent, non-required @RequestParam binds to null, not to an empty string.
Trace which branch of the if statement executes for each call, based on whether category is null or has a real value.
exercises.expectedAnswer: GET /search with no query string calls productService.findAll(), because category is not provided and required=false lets the request through with category bound to null, taking the if-branch. GET /search?category=shoes calls productService.findByCategory("shoes"), because category is now bound to the string "shoes", which is not null, so the if-branch is skipped.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because category is declared @RequestParam(required = false) and there is no defaultValue, an omitted category query parameter does not cause a 400 error. It leaves category bound to null (with a primitive such as int, the same request would fail with a 500, because null cannot be assigned to it; use Integer for optional numbers). The method's own if (category == null) check then explicitly branches to productService.findAll() for that case. When category=shoes is supplied in the query string, Spring binds the literal string "shoes" to the parameter, category is no longer null, and the method falls through to productService.findByCategory("shoes") instead. Both calls hit the same search method; only the bound value differs.

assessments.prompt: Two handler methods in the same controller are both mapped with @PostMapping("/items/{id}") -- identical path pattern and identical HTTP method, but different parameter types. What happens when the application starts?
options: Spring disambiguates the two methods based on their different parameter types, similar to Java method overload resolution.
The first-defined method silently wins and the second is ignored at runtime.
Both methods run in sequence for every matching request, and their return values are merged.
The application fails to start with an ambiguous mapping error.
assessments.explanation: Spring's request mapping matches based on path pattern shape, HTTP method, and any explicitly declared conditions like headers/params/consumes/produces. It has no concept of Java method overload resolution and does not consider parameter types or names when deciding whether two mappings conflict. Because both mappings here are identical in every dimension Spring checks, this is detected as a conflict while the handler index is built at startup, and the application fails to start with an Ambiguous mapping error. The “Spring disambiguates the two methods based…”, “The first-defined method silently wins…”, and “Both methods run in sequence for every…” options each describe behavior Spring MVC does not implement.

assessments.prompt: A handler is declared `@GetMapping("/orders") public List<Order> listOrders(@RequestParam String status)`, with no `required` attribute set and no `defaultValue` given. A client sends `GET /orders` with no query string at all. What happens?
options: The request is rejected with a 400 Bad Request.
status is bound to an empty string "", and listOrders executes normally.
status is bound to null, and listOrders executes normally.
Spring treats the missing parameter as a routing mismatch and returns 404 Not Found instead of invoking listOrders.
assessments.explanation: @RequestParam's `required` attribute defaults to true, and when a required parameter with no defaultValue is missing from the request entirely, Spring rejects the request with 400 Bad Request before the handler method ever runs. This is the opposite of the @RequestParam(required = false) pattern shown in the module's examples, where required is explicitly set to false to allow omission. The “status is bound to null, and listOrders executes normally” and “status is bound to an empty string…” options describe what would happen if required were explicitly false (null), but the “status is bound to an empty string…” option's empty-string claim is wrong even then, since an absent parameter binds to null, not "". The “Spring treats the missing parameter…” option is wrong because the path itself still matches perfectly; the failure is in parameter resolution, not routing.

assessments.prompt: A controller registers only `@PostMapping("/orders")`. A client sends `GET /orders` against that exact path. What HTTP status is returned, and why?
options: 404 Not Found, because no registered handler's path pattern matches the request at all.
405 Method Not Allowed, because a mapping's path matches, but no handler registered for that path accepts the GET method.
400 Bad Request, because the request itself is considered malformed.
500 Internal Server Error, because DispatcherServlet cannot resolve any handler for the request, and reports that as a server error.
assessments.explanation: A request path that matches no registered pattern at all gets a plain 404, but a path that DOES match (just not for the HTTP method used) gets the more specific 405 Method Not Allowed, since the resource clearly exists, just not for that verb. Here, /orders matches the registered @PostMapping's path exactly, so it's the method mismatch (GET vs the registered POST) that triggers 405, not a routing miss. The “404 Not Found, because no registered handler's…” option is wrong because the path does match something. The “400 Bad Request, because the request itself…” and “500 Internal Server Error, because DispatcherServlet cannot…” options describe failures unrelated to this specific mismatch between a matched path and an unsupported method.

assessments.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between @RestController and @Controller?
options: @RestController is a completely separate mechanism unrelated to @Controller, built specifically for microservice architectures.
@RestController disables Spring's HandlerMapping-based routing entirely, requiring requests to be dispatched manually.
@RestController is a meta-annotation combining @Controller with @ResponseBody.
@RestController is only necessary when a controller class declares more than one handler method.
assessments.explanation: @RestController exists purely to remove the repetition of writing @Controller plus @ResponseBody on every handler method in a class where every method produces a body rather than a view. The “@RestController is a completely separate mechanism unrelated…” option is false because @RestController is itself annotated with @Controller. The “@RestController disables Spring's HandlerMapping-based routing entirely, requiring…” option is false: routing through DispatcherServlet and its HandlerMapping index works identically regardless of which of the two stereotypes is used. The “@RestController is only necessary when a controller…” option is false: the choice between @Controller and @RestController has nothing to do with how many handler methods a class happens to declare.

assessments.prompt: Explain, step by step, how DispatcherServlet decides which method handles a given incoming HTTP request in a Spring Boot REST application.
assessments.modelAnswer: Spring MVC follows the front controller pattern: a single DispatcherServlet, registered automatically by Spring Boot's web autoconfiguration once a web starter is on the classpath, is the one servlet that receives every incoming HTTP request for the application, rather than each controller registering its own separate servlet. At application startup, before any request has been handled, Spring inspects every @Controller/@RestController bean in the context and indexes each of its @RequestMapping-family-annotated methods (including the @GetMapping/@PostMapping/etc. shortcuts, which are just @RequestMapping specialized to one HTTP method) into a HandlerMapping, recording each method's path pattern, HTTP method, and any additional declared conditions such as consumes, produces, headers, or params. When a HTTP request arrives, DispatcherServlet asks this HandlerMapping to find the single best match for the request's path and method (and any other conditions that were specified), and dispatches control to that one handler method, later passing the return value through the registered HttpMessageConverter chain to produce the response body. If no mapping's path matches at all, the client gets a 404; if the path matches but no handler there accepts the request's HTTP method, the client gets a 405. Because the index is built at startup, two methods declaring the same path-and-method mapping stop the application from starting. Patterns that differ only in variable names slip past that check and fail as ambiguous when a request matches both.

concepts.title: Request and Response Bodies: JSON Binding
concepts.description: @RequestBody and the @ResponseBody behavior already implied by @RestController delegate the actual work of converting between JSON on the wire and Java objects in memory to Jackson's HttpMessageConverter, and understanding exactly how that conversion works explains a large share of the 400 and 500 errors you'll encounter building REST APIs.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of HttpMessageConverter and how Jackson's converter becomes available via autoconfiguration.
Use @RequestBody to deserialize an incoming JSON body into a Java object, and explain what determines field mapping.
Explain what happens, and what happens NOT to happen, when incoming JSON has extra or missing fields relative to the target class.
Explain why a malformed or type-mismatched JSON body causes a 400 error before the controller method body ever executes.
Use @JsonProperty to decouple a wire-format field name from the Java field name.
Explain the role of the Content-Type and Accept headers in selecting which HttpMessageConverter handles a request or response.

sections.heading: HttpMessageConverter: The Thing That Actually Converts JSON
sections.body:
`@RequestBody` (for reading) and `@ResponseBody` (for writing, already implied by `@RestController` on every method) are instructions to Spring MVC: 'do not treat this as a plain request parameter or a view name; run it through the registered `HttpMessageConverter` chain instead.' `HttpMessageConverter` is the abstraction responsible for the actual conversion between raw HTTP bytes and a Java object. `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` (the one that handles JSON) is registered automatically the moment Jackson's classes are present on the classpath, which happens because `spring-boot-starter-web` transitively brings in `jackson-databind` and `JacksonAutoConfiguration`'s `@ConditionalOnClass` check for Jackson's classes passes.

Which converter gets used for a given request is not arbitrary: for reading a `@RequestBody`, Spring picks a converter that can handle the request's declared `Content-Type` header; for writing a response, it picks one based on the request's `Accept` header (and any `produces` value declared on the mapping). In Spring Boot 4, which defaults to Jackson 3, the equivalent class is `JacksonJsonHttpMessageConverter`; what follows applies to both unless noted.

sections.heading: Deserializing @RequestBody: How Jackson Maps JSON to Java
When Deserialization Genuinely Fails: 400 via HttpMessageNotReadableException
sections.body:
If the JSON itself is not syntactically valid, or if a JSON value cannot be coerced into the type the target field declares (a JSON string `"yes"` where the target field is a `boolean`, for instance, since of all JSON strings Jackson coerces only spellings of true and false such as `"true"`, `"True"` or `"FALSE"`), Jackson throws a mapping/parsing exception, which Spring MVC catches and wraps into `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, automatically translated into an HTTP `400 Bad Request` response, before your controller method's body ever runs.

A body that fails to even become a valid object (bad JSON syntax, an incompatible type) fails at the *conversion* layer, via `HttpMessageNotReadableException`. A body that parses and converts successfully, but violates a *business* rule (a blank required name, a negative price) is a different kind of failure, caught by Bean Validation on an object that DOES exist, which is what the next concept covers.

sections.heading: Decoupling Wire Format From Java Naming With @JsonProperty
sections.body: A REST API's JSON field names do not have to match your Java field names: API consumers might reasonably expect `snake_case` (a common convention in many ecosystems) while idiomatic Java uses `camelCase`. `@JsonProperty("customer_name")` on a `customerName` field tells Jackson to use `customer_name` as the logical property name on the wire, in *both* directions: deserializing an incoming `customer_name` key correctly populates the Java field, and serializing that field for an outgoing response emits `customer_name`, not `customerName`. A Java-side rename then doesn't become a breaking API change. Two related annotations: `@JsonIgnore` excludes a field (like a password hash) from being serialized (and from being read in; use `@JsonProperty(access = WRITE_ONLY)` for a password you accept but never return), and `@JsonFormat` controls how a date/time value is rendered on the wire.

sections.heading: Content Negotiation: Accept, Content-Type, and produces/consumes
sections.body: The request's `Content-Type` header tells Spring MVC what format the *incoming* body is in, which determines which `HttpMessageConverter` is even considered capable of reading it: a request declaring `Content-Type: application/json` is read by the Jackson converter; a mapping restricted with `consumes = "application/json"` will reject any other content type outright with `415 Unsupported Media Type`, before deserialization is even attempted. Separately, the request's `Accept` header (and any `produces` value declared on the mapping) governs which converter is used to *write* the response, and therefore what `Content-Type` the response itself carries. If a client sends `Accept: application/xml` and the application has no XML converter registered (the common case, unless an XML library is explicitly added), Spring MVC cannot satisfy that request and responds with `406 Not Acceptable`. That differs from a routing 404: the path and method matched, but nothing on the server can produce the requested representation.

examples.title: A Basic @RequestBody / Response Round-Trip
examples.explanation: Because the request declares Content-Type: application/json, Spring MVC selects MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter to read the body. Jackson constructs a CreateOrderRequest via its no-argument constructor, then calls setCustomerName("Amy") and setItems([...]) via reflection, matching each JSON key to a same-named Java property. By the time createOrder's body runs, request is a fully populated, ordinary Java object: the controller method itself never touches JSON directly. The Order object it returns goes back out through the same converter machinery in reverse, serialized to JSON for the response body, with its own Content-Type chosen based on the incoming request's Accept header.

examples.title: Silent Data Loss From a Typo'd JSON Key
examples.explanation: The JSON key is custName, not customerName: a typo. The payload is valid JSON, and Spring Boot's mapper ignores unrecognized keys, so custName is dropped and customerName stays null, as it would on any newly constructed object whose setter was never called. The request succeeds with 200 OK and no exception anywhere, producing an incomplete object. Bean Validation (the next concept) closes this gap: a @NotBlank constraint on customerName would catch the null and reject the request with a clear 400, where deserialization alone sees nothing wrong.

examples.title: Renaming Fields for the Wire With @JsonProperty
examples.explanation: @JsonProperty configures the logical wire-format name for a property in both directions at once: deserialization recognizes customer_name as the key for the customerName field (rather than expecting a literal customerName key), and serialization emits customer_name rather than customerName when writing this object back out as a response. The Java field names stay idiomatic camelCase throughout the codebase: renaming a Java field later leaves the JSON contract alone, as long as the @JsonProperty value stays.

misconceptions.description: If the incoming JSON doesn't exactly match the target Java class's fields, Spring will reject the request with an error -- extra or missing fields are treated as invalid input.
misconceptions.clarification: By default, Spring Boot's Jackson configuration disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, so JSON keys with no matching Java property are ignored, and any Java field with no corresponding JSON value is left at its ordinary default (null, 0, false). Neither raises an exception on its own. This leniency is convenient for API evolution (older clients sending fewer fields, or newer clients sending extra ones, don't break), but a typo'd key produces an incomplete object rather than an error, which is why validation matters: it inspects the object AFTER deserialization and can catch the null field.

misconceptions.description: A malformed JSON body and a body that violates a business validation rule (like a blank required field) both fail for essentially the same reason and produce the same kind of error.
misconceptions.clarification: They are different failures from different layers. A body that is not valid JSON, or that can't be coerced into the target type's declared field types (a string where a boolean is expected, for example), fails during CONVERSION: Jackson throws a mapping exception, Spring wraps it as HttpMessageNotReadableException, and your controller method's body never runs at all, because the target object was never constructed. A body that IS valid JSON and DOES convert successfully, but leaves a field blank that a business rule requires to be non-blank, fails during VALIDATION: Bean Validation runs against a fully-constructed object and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException. Both commonly map to a 400 status by default, but they are different exception types, so a centralized error handler needs a method for each.

exercises.prompt: A POST request to create a product fails with a 400 error before ProductController's method body ever executes, even though the Java class below compiles fine and looks correctly annotated. Given the request body shown, explain why deserialization fails and fix the JSON payload so the request succeeds.
hints: Look specifically at the inStock field's declared Java type versus the JSON value supplied for it.
Jackson's boolean coercion from a JSON string only recognizes spellings of the words "true" and "false" -- what happens when the string is neither?
This failure happens during @RequestBody conversion, before createProduct's body runs at all -- fixing it means fixing the JSON value's type, not anything inside the controller method.
exercises.solutionExplanation: inStock is declared as a Java boolean, but the client sent the JSON string "yes" for it. Jackson's boolean deserializer accepts the JSON values true/false, integers (0 is false, anything else true), and strings such as "true", "True" or "FALSE". "yes" is none of these, so Jackson throws InvalidFormatException while trying to convert the request body into a ProductRequest object. Spring MVC wraps that into HttpMessageNotReadableException, which is automatically translated into a 400 Bad Request response, and because the ProductRequest object was never successfully constructed, createProduct's method body never runs. A breakpoint in the controller would never be hit; the server log shows the Jackson message naming the field. Sending the JSON boolean literal true for inStock fixes the request.

exercises.prompt: Given this class, controller method, and request body, what does the HTTP response's status and body say, and why doesn't Spring reject the request even though 'custName' doesn't match any field on CreateOrderRequest?
hints: Is "custName" valid JSON syntax? Does it fail to convert into any type at all, or does it just fail to MATCH anything on the target class?
Recall that Spring Boot's Jackson configuration disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES by default -- what does Jackson do with a JSON key it doesn't recognize?
If customerName is never set by any key in the payload, what value does that field hold by the time createOrder's body runs?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 200 OK, with the response body 'Order for: null'. The JSON is syntactically valid and 'custName' doesn't cause an error because Spring Boot's Jackson autoconfiguration disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES by default -- an unrecognized key is simply ignored rather than rejected. Since no key in the payload matches customerName, that field is never set and defaults to null, so request.getCustomerName() returns null and the concatenated string is 'Order for: null'.
exercises.solutionExplanation: "custName" is valid JSON and doesn't correspond to any declared property on CreateOrderRequest, but Spring Boot's mapper has FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES disabled (a plain Jackson 2 ObjectMapper has it enabled), so the key is ignored. Because customerName was never populated by any key in this particular payload, it keeps its default value of null once the object is constructed. createOrder's body runs normally, and Java string concatenation turns the null reference into the text "null". The response is 200 OK with the body "Order for: null", the kind of bug @NotBlank (next concept) catches.

assessments.prompt: A POST request's JSON body contains "quantity": "abc" for a field declared as `private int quantity;` on the target @RequestBody class. What is the most accurate description of what happens?
options: The server returns a 500 Internal Server Error because this is an unhandled server-side bug.
quantity is set to 0 (int's default value), and the controller method runs normally.
The request fails with a 400 Bad Request via HttpMessageNotReadableException.
A NumberFormatException is thrown inside the controller method when quantity is first used.
assessments.explanation: Jackson cannot coerce the JSON string "abc" into an int, so it throws a mapping exception during deserialization, which Spring MVC wraps as HttpMessageNotReadableException and automatically translates into a 400 Bad Request. This happens during argument resolution, before the controller method's body ever runs, so the “A NumberFormatException is thrown inside the controller…” option is wrong (the method body never gets a chance to touch quantity at all) and the “quantity is set to 0…” option is wrong (defaults apply to OMITTED fields, not mismatched ones). The “The server returns a 500 Internal Server…” option is wrong because this is a client input problem, correctly surfaced as a 4xx client error, not a 5xx server fault.

assessments.prompt: Plain Jackson 2 (used outside of Spring Boot) has FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES enabled by default, meaning an unrecognized JSON key throws an exception during deserialization. What does Spring Boot's own Jackson autoconfiguration do differently, and why does that matter in practice?
options: Spring Boot explicitly disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, so unrecognized keys are silently ignored -- convenient for API evolution across client versions, but it also means a typo'd JSON key produces a silently incomplete object rather than a clear, immediate error.
Spring Boot only disables this check when running under a test profile, leaving it enabled in production.
Spring Boot replaces Jackson entirely with its own JSON parser that has no concept of unknown-key detection at all.
Spring Boot leaves the setting exactly as vanilla Jackson has it, so unknown JSON keys still throw an exception inside a Spring Boot application.
assessments.explanation: Spring Boot's Jackson autoconfiguration turns off FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, where plain Jackson 2 has it on. Older or newer API clients sending slightly different field sets don't break, but a typo'd key like "custName" instead of "customerName" leaves the intended field null with no error, so a mistake that a strict mapper would surface goes unnoticed. The “Spring Boot leaves the setting exactly…” option describes vanilla Jackson's behavior, not Spring Boot's. The “Spring Boot replaces Jackson entirely…” and “Spring Boot only disables this check…” options invent behaviors: this is a single feature flag, the same in every profile.

assessments.prompt: A mapping is declared `@PostMapping(value = "/orders", consumes = "application/json")`. A client sends a request to that path with header `Content-Type: application/xml` and an XML body. What happens?
options: Spring attempts to parse the XML body as if it were JSON, and the request likely fails with a deserialization error inside the handler.
Spring automatically transcodes the XML body into an equivalent JSON structure before continuing to the handler.
The request proceeds normally, since `consumes` only restricts what a mapping can produce as a response, not what it can accept as a request body.
The request is rejected with 415 Unsupported Media Type before any deserialization is attempted.
assessments.explanation: The `consumes` attribute on a mapping restricts which request Content-Types that handler will accept at all: a mismatch is detected before Spring even attempts to select an HttpMessageConverter to read the body, and the client gets 415 Unsupported Media Type. The “Spring attempts to parse the XML body…” option is wrong because Spring never blindly attempts cross-format parsing; the content-type check happens first and short-circuits that entirely. The “Spring automatically transcodes the XML body into…” option describes automatic transcoding that Spring MVC does not perform. The “The request proceeds normally, since `consumes` only…” option inverts the actual roles of `consumes` (governs acceptable request bodies) and `produces` (governs response representation).

assessments.prompt: A Java field is declared `@JsonProperty("customer_name") private String customerName;`. Which statement about this annotation's effect is correct?
options: It only affects serialization when writing a response; incoming JSON must still use the key `customerName` to populate the field.
It affects both directions at once: incoming JSON must use the key `customer_name` to populate the field, and outgoing JSON serializes the field back out under the key `customer_name` as well.
It has no effect at all unless FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is also disabled on the same class.
It only affects deserialization of incoming JSON; outgoing responses still emit the key `customerName`.
assessments.explanation: @JsonProperty configures the logical wire-format name for a property in both directions simultaneously: deserialization recognizes `customer_name` as the key that populates `customerName`, and serialization emits `customer_name` (not the Java field's own name) when writing the object back out as a response. The Java field can then be renamed without touching the API contract. The “It only affects serialization when writing…” and “It only affects deserialization of incoming JSON…” options each describe only one direction, which understates what the annotation does. The “It has no effect at all unless…” option incorrectly ties @JsonProperty's effect to an unrelated Jackson feature flag.

assessments.prompt: Explain, step by step, what happens from the moment an HTTP POST request with a JSON body arrives at a Spring Boot application to the moment a @RequestBody-annotated parameter is a fully populated Java object -- and explain what happens instead if the JSON can't be mapped onto the target type.
assessments.modelAnswer: When a POST request arrives, DispatcherServlet routes it to the matching handler method based on path and HTTP method, as with any other request. Once a handler method is selected, Spring MVC inspects its parameters and finds one annotated @RequestBody, which tells it not to treat that parameter as a plain request parameter but instead to resolve it by reading the raw request body through the registered HttpMessageConverter chain. It selects a converter capable of handling the request's declared Content-Type: for application/json, that's MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, present because Jackson was autoconfigured onto the classpath by the web starter. That converter delegates to Jackson's ObjectMapper, which parses the JSON text and attempts to construct an instance of the target class, typically via its no-argument constructor, then populates it by matching each JSON key to a same-named Java property and calling the corresponding setter (or field, depending on configuration): keys with no matching property are ignored by default under Spring Boot's Jackson settings, and any property with no matching key is left at its default value. If every step of this succeeds, the fully populated object is handed to the controller method as the value of its @RequestBody parameter, and the method body executes normally. If, instead, the JSON is not syntactically valid, or a value can't be coerced into its target field's type (a string where a number or boolean is expected, for instance), Jackson throws a parsing or mapping exception partway through this process; Spring MVC catches that and wraps it as HttpMessageNotReadableException, which by default is translated automatically into an HTTP 400 Bad Request response, and the controller method is never invoked.

concepts.title: Request Validation and Centralized Exception Handling
concepts.description: @Valid triggers Bean Validation against constraint annotations like @NotBlank and @Min on an already-deserialized request object, and @ExceptionHandler / @ControllerAdvice let you translate both those validation failures and any other exception into one consistent, centralized error response instead of scattering try/catch blocks across every controller method.
learningObjectives: Explain what triggers Bean Validation on a @RequestBody parameter and what exception a failed validation throws.
Apply constraint annotations (@NotBlank, @NotNull, @NotEmpty, @Size, @Min/@Max) to a request DTO and correctly distinguish between them.
Explain Spring Boot's default, uncentralized error response and why it's unsuitable for a real API's clients.
Write an @ExceptionHandler method and explain how @ControllerAdvice scopes it globally instead of to a single controller.
Explain the precedence rule Spring uses when multiple @ExceptionHandler methods could apply to a thrown exception.
Design a consistent error response shape and justify why consistency across every endpoint matters for API consumers.

sections.heading: Triggering Validation: @Valid and MethodArgumentNotValidException
sections.body:
Placing `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` parameter tells Spring MVC to run Bean Validation (the JSR/Jakarta Bean Validation specification, implemented by Hibernate Validator) against that object's declared constraint annotations, but only *after* Jackson has deserialized the JSON into that object. A body that Jackson can't parse or coerce fails earlier, during conversion, as `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, and validation never runs.

`@Valid` on the parameter covers that object's own fields. To validate a nested object, put `@Valid` on the nested field too; forgetting this is a common reason nested constraints appear to be ignored.

Since Spring Boot 2.3, Bean Validation is no longer pulled in by `spring-boot-starter-web`; add `spring-boot-starter-validation`. Without it the `jakarta.validation` imports don't compile. Worse, if another library brings in the annotations (the API jar) without Hibernate Validator, everything compiles and the constraints are ignored at runtime. When validation does run and finds one or more violated constraints, Spring throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which carries a `BindingResult` containing *every* violated field and its message, not just the first failure encountered, so a client can, in principle, be told about every problem with their request in a single response instead of fixing one field at a time through repeated round trips.

sections.heading: Constraint Annotations: @NotNull, @NotEmpty, @NotBlank
Default Error Behavior Without Any Centralized Handling
sections.body: Without any custom exception handling at all, an exception (`MethodArgumentNotValidException` from a failed `@Valid` check, or a `RuntimeException` from a service) ends up in Spring Boot's own built-in default error handling (`BasicErrorController`, backing the `/error` path every Spring Boot web app registers automatically), which produces a generic JSON body containing fields like `timestamp`, `status`, `error`, and `path`. This is a poor fit for an API whose clients need to react to errors: for a validation failure it doesn't say which fields failed, and it carries no application-specific code or message (Spring Boot leaves `message` out by default so internals don't leak). You can switch on Spring's RFC 9457 problem-details format with `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`, or centralize error handling yourself, covered next.

sections.heading: @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice
Matching Precedence Among Multiple Handlers
sections.body:
When more than one `@ExceptionHandler` method could technically apply to a thrown exception (because the exception's class hierarchy matches more than one declared handler type), Spring runs only one. Within a class it selects the handler whose declared exception type is the *closest* match in the thrown exception's type hierarchy. In the example above, a thrown `MethodArgumentNotValidException` technically matches both `handleValidation` (declared for that exact type) and `handleGeneric` (declared for `Exception`, an ancestor of everything), but `handleValidation` wins as the closer match.

Across classes the rule is different. A handler in the controller itself beats any `@ControllerAdvice`. With several advice classes, Spring tries them in `@Order` order and uses the first one that has *any* match, so a high-priority advice with an `Exception` handler can shadow a more specific handler in another class. Keep the catch-all in the lowest-priority advice.

examples.title: A Validated Request DTO
examples.explanation: @Valid on the parameter tells Spring to run Bean Validation against the CreateOrderRequest instance immediately after Jackson has built it. If customerName is blank, items is empty (or contains a blank string, thanks to the container-element constraint List<@NotBlank String>), or quantity is less than 1, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException carrying every one of those violations at once, and createOrder's body never executes. A request that omits quantity fails too: the primitive int defaults to 0, which violates @Min(1).

examples.title: Centralizing Error Handling With @RestControllerAdvice
examples.explanation: This class governs error responses for every controller. handleValidation walks the BindingResult's field errors and assembles a map of field name to message, giving API consumers a structured, machine-parseable object to branch on (e.g., to highlight the exact form fields that failed) rather than a single generic error string. If one field violates two constraints, the map keeps only the last message; use a list per field if clients need all of them. handleNotFound does the same for a domain exception, with its own status code and message.

examples.title: The Default Error Response vs. a Centralized One
examples.explanation: The default response confirms that something was wrong, but not WHICH fields failed or why, so a client can't show 'Customer name is required' next to the right form field. The centralized version, built from the same exception's BindingResult, exposes which fields failed and with what message, in a shape that is the same across every endpoint. That consistency is the real payoff of centralizing: not just less duplicated code, but one predictable contract that every client of the API can rely on, instead of an ad hoc shape depending on which corner of the codebase threw.

misconceptions.description: An @ExceptionHandler method only catches exceptions thrown inside the exact same method it's declared alongside, similar to a try/catch wrapped tightly around one specific call.
misconceptions.clarification: An @ExceptionHandler method declared inside a controller class applies to every handler method within that ENTIRE controller class, not just one. Declared inside a @ControllerAdvice (or @RestControllerAdvice) class instead, it applies GLOBALLY, to any matching exception thrown anywhere during request handling across the whole application, including exceptions Spring itself throws internally, like MethodArgumentNotValidException during argument resolution, not only exceptions your own code throws.
misconceptions.fact: An @ExceptionHandler method declared inside a controller class applies to every handler method within that ENTIRE controller class, not just one.

misconceptions.description: As long as there's a generic @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) registered somewhere, it doesn't matter whether you also add a more specific handler for MethodArgumentNotValidException -- the generic one will catch it too, so the specific one is redundant.
misconceptions.clarification: It's true that a generic Exception handler WOULD technically match a thrown MethodArgumentNotValidException, since it's a subtype of Exception, but Spring's handler resolution always prefers the MOST SPECIFIC applicable handler when more than one is registered, so a dedicated MethodArgumentNotValidException handler, if present, wins over a generic one in the same advice class. It isn't redundant: the specific handler has typed access to ex.getBindingResult() and its field errors, which a generic Exception handler would need an instanceof check and cast to reach.

exercises.prompt: Add validation constraints to this DTO so that a request is rejected -- before the controller method body runs -- if email is blank or not a valid email address, or if quantity is less than 1. Then wire @Valid into the controller method so those constraints actually get enforced.
hints: You'll need constraint annotations from jakarta.validation.constraints -- specifically something for 'must not be blank', something for 'must look like an email', and something for 'must be at least a given number'.

Field-level constraint annotations alone do nothing on their own -- Spring only actually runs Bean Validation against an object if the method parameter using it is explicitly marked to trigger validation.
The annotation that triggers validation goes on the @RequestBody parameter itself, not on the class definition.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @NotBlank rejects a null, empty, or all-whitespace email, and @Email additionally checks that whatever non-blank value IS supplied looks like a valid email address: both are needed, since @Email accepts null and the empty string, and @NotBlank says nothing about the value's shape. @Min(1) on quantity rejects zero and negative values, and an omitted quantity too, because a primitive int defaults to 0. None of these annotations do anything by themselves: Bean Validation only runs against the constructed SubscriptionRequest object because @Valid was added to the @RequestBody parameter in the controller method; without it, the constraints compile but are never checked.

exercises.prompt: A team centralizes error handling with the class below. When OrderNotFoundException is thrown, clients report NOT getting the clean JSON error body the team expected. Explain what's actually going wrong and fix the class.
hints: @ControllerAdvice by itself does NOT imply @ResponseBody -- compare this to the difference between plain @Controller and @RestController.
Without @ResponseBody in effect, Spring MVC treats a handler method's return value the same way it would for any ordinary @Controller method -- built around producing a view, not a REST body.
There are two valid fixes: add @ResponseBody to the handler method itself, or change the class-level annotation to @RestControllerAdvice, which already bundles @ResponseBody in.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Plain @ControllerAdvice does not carry @ResponseBody the way @RestControllerAdvice does. Its handler methods follow the same return-value rules as plain @Controller methods, and there a returned Map is treated as model attributes for a view. With no view name given, Spring derives one from the request path (GET /orders/42 looks for a view called orders/42), finds no such template, and the client gets an error page or the generic error JSON. Switching the class annotation to @RestControllerAdvice (or, equivalently, keeping @ControllerAdvice but adding @ResponseBody directly on handleNotFound) makes Spring MVC write the Map to the response body as JSON. @ResponseStatus supplies the 404; without it the body would say 404 while the HTTP status stayed 200.

assessments.prompt: A @RestControllerAdvice class defines an @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class) and also an @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class). A controller method throws a NumberFormatException, which is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException. Which handler method actually runs?
options: The IllegalArgumentException handler, because Spring selects the most specific matching handler in the exception's type hierarchy.
The Exception handler, because it was declared to catch every possible exception type.
Both handlers run in sequence, with the more specific one running first.
The application fails to start because two handlers can both technically match the same exception.
assessments.explanation: Spring's exception-handler resolution picks the closest matching type in the thrown exception's class hierarchy, not the first one declared or the most general one available. NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException, which is a far closer match than the generic Exception ancestor, so the IllegalArgumentException-specific handler runs. The “The Exception handler, because it was declared…” option misunderstands the resolution rule: a generic handler only runs when nothing more specific matches. The “Both handlers run in sequence…” option is wrong because exactly one handler runs per exception, never a chained sequence of matching handlers. The “The application fails to start because two…” option is wrong: a general handler alongside a more specific one is valid; only two handlers for the same exception type in one class are ambiguous.

assessments.prompt: A field is annotated @NotEmpty (not @NotBlank). A request supplies the value "   " (three whitespace characters) for that field. What happens?
options: Validation fails, but only because the string exceeds some implicit default maximum length.
@NotEmpty cannot be applied to a String field at all -- it only applies to collections.
Validation passes, because @NotEmpty only requires a length greater than zero, and a whitespace-only string has non-zero length even though its trimmed content is empty.
Validation fails, because @NotEmpty rejects whitespace-only strings the exact same way @NotBlank does.
assessments.explanation: @NotNull rejects only a null reference, @NotEmpty additionally requires a size/length greater than zero (so null and "" fail, but "   " passes, since it technically has non-zero length), and @NotBlank alone requires a trimmed length greater than zero, which is the only one of the three that would reject "   ". Since this field uses @NotEmpty, the whitespace-only value passes. The “Validation fails, because @NotEmpty rejects whitespace-only strings…” option wrongly conflates @NotEmpty with the stricter @NotBlank. The “Validation fails, but only because the string…” option invents a length ceiling that doesn't exist in the constraint's actual semantics. The “@NotEmpty cannot be applied to a String…” option is wrong: @NotEmpty supports strings (any CharSequence), collections, maps and arrays.

assessments.prompt: A Spring Boot 3 application adds @Valid and @NotBlank annotations to a request DTO. It uses spring-boot-starter-web, and the annotations come from a jakarta.validation-api jar that another library happens to bring in; no other validation-related dependency is present. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The application fails to compile, because @NotBlank requires a dedicated annotation processor that must be configured manually.

The constraint annotations have nothing to actually execute against, because since Spring Boot 2.3, Bean Validation support is no longer pulled in transitively by spring-boot-starter-web -- spring-boot-starter-validation must be added explicitly.
Validation works exactly as intended, since spring-boot-starter-web transitively includes Hibernate Validator in every Spring Boot version.
Spring silently substitutes its own internal validation engine that ignores Jakarta Bean Validation annotations like @NotBlank entirely.
assessments.explanation: Since Spring Boot 2.3, spring-boot-starter-web no longer pulls in Hibernate Validator, so @Valid has nothing to run against unless spring-boot-starter-validation is added. Here the API jar makes the annotations compile (ruling out the “The application fails to compile, because @NotBlank…” option), but nothing evaluates them at runtime. With no API jar either, the imports would not compile, though for lack of the dependency rather than an annotation processor. The “Validation works exactly as intended, since spring-boot-starter-web…” option describes the pre-2.3 behavior, not the current one. The “Spring silently substitutes its own internal validation…” option is wrong because Spring Boot has no Bean Validation implementation of its own.

assessments.prompt: An @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class) method is declared directly inside OrderController itself, not inside a @ControllerAdvice class. A completely different controller, PaymentController, also throws OrderNotFoundException from one of its own handler methods. What happens when that exception is thrown from PaymentController?
options: PaymentController automatically inherits OrderController's exception handlers, as long as both classes live in the same package.
OrderController's handler catches it there too, because @ExceptionHandler methods apply application-wide by default, regardless of where they're declared.
The application fails to start, because the same exception type cannot legally be handled in more than one place across the codebase.

The exception is NOT caught by OrderController's handler -- a controller-level @ExceptionHandler only applies to handler methods within that same controller class, so it instead propagates to Spring Boot's default error handling (or a matching @ControllerAdvice, if one exists).
assessments.explanation: A controller-level @ExceptionHandler's scope is that controller class, so PaymentController's thrown OrderNotFoundException never reaches OrderController's handler at all; it propagates upward to whatever broader handling exists (a @ControllerAdvice, if one is registered, or otherwise Spring Boot's own default error handling). The “OrderController's handler catches it there too…” option directly contradicts the controller-scoped nature of a plain @ExceptionHandler. The “The application fails to start…” option is false: multiple classes can legitimately declare handlers for the same exception type at different scopes. The “PaymentController automatically inherits OrderController's exception handlers…” option invents an inheritance mechanism that Spring does not provide.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer who currently handles errors with a try/catch block inside every controller method why moving to @Valid plus a centralized @RestControllerAdvice is a better approach, and describe specifically what changes in the flow of a request that fails validation.
assessments.modelAnswer: With try/catch scattered across every controller method, each method is individually responsible for deciding what counts as invalid input, checking for it manually, and formatting its own error response, so the shape of an error (which fields appear, what a client can rely on) drifts between endpoints, and every method carries repetitive validation and error-formatting code that has nothing to do with its actual business logic. Moving validation into declarative constraint annotations (@NotBlank, @Min, and so on) on the request DTO, combined with @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter, removes that manual checking: Spring runs Bean Validation automatically, immediately after the object is deserialized and before the controller method body executes at all. If any constraint fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException carrying every violated field and its message, and the controller method's body never runs. That exception then propagates up to a single @RestControllerAdvice class's @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) method, the one place that turns it into a response body, so every endpoint produces the same error shape and API clients can write one piece of error handling. The method bodies also lose their defensive checks, because by the time they run, @Valid has already guaranteed the constraints hold. The net effect is less code, written once, and a contract clients can build on.

assessments.prompt: Your API returns a raw 500 with a stack trace when a client sends an order with a negative quantity, and different controllers format errors differently. How would you fix both problems?
assessments.modelAnswer: Validate input at the boundary: annotate the request DTO fields (for example @Positive on quantity, @NotBlank on required strings) and add @Valid to the @RequestBody parameter so invalid input is rejected before business logic runs. Then centralise error handling in a @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods that map MethodArgumentNotValidException to 400 with field-level messages, domain exceptions such as OrderNotFoundException to 404, and unexpected exceptions to a generic 500 that logs the details server-side without leaking stack traces. Use one consistent error body, ideally ProblemDetail (RFC 9457, formerly RFC 7807), which Spring supports since 6.0, so every controller returns the same shape. Add MockMvc tests asserting the status and body for invalid input so the contract stays stable.
